a1_answer:
MECHANISM CLASS: In-situ conductivity trend-inference from existing water quality logs, paired with a scheduled thermal-flush operating-point shift on existing fan and water-system equipment.

NOVELTY STATEMENT
Standard practice: Periodic visual inspection of the fill or online turbidity/pH/conductivity sensor insertion into the water loop to detect fouling onset.
Departure: Infer fill-fouling state exclusively from the rate of change of bulk water conductivity (existing log) and the thermal approach (existing T_in/T_out), and mitigate by commanding a temporary thermal-flush duty cycle (high flow, high heat rejection) using existing variable-speed drives and controls.
Failure-physics connection: Scaling deposition rate is proportional to the supersaturation index of dissolved ions; as the fill fouls, the effective heat-transfer area degrades, causing the approach (T_out − T_water,inlet) to rise for a fixed load. Simultaneously, fouling traps ions locally, altering bulk conductivity trends. A sudden spike in conductivity gradient or a drift in the approach-conductivity correlation indicates critical fouling. The thermal flush physically scrubs the surface by inducing high shear and thermal shock, reversing the fouling layer before the approach trips.

PHYSICS CHECK
Governing relation: $\frac{d(\Delta T)}{dt} = f(\dot{m}, \Delta H, A_{eff})$, where $A_{eff}$ is the effective heat transfer area. Fouling reduces $A_{eff}$, so $\Delta T$ (approach) increases. Conductivity $\sigma$ correlates with ion concentration in the bulk; fouling alters local saturation, causing measurable drift in $d\sigma/dt$.
Magnitude verification: For a 35 C approach design, a 10% loss in effective area due to fouling increases the required approach by ~1.5–2 C. This shift is well above the 0.1 C resolution of standard RTD temperature sensors already in the system. Conductivity drift of >5% over 24h is a standard early-warning indicator for scaling precursors in cooling water loops.
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = supersaturation index / local ion concentration; the mechanism moves it DOWN by inducing thermal shock and high-shear flushing via existing flow/heat rejection modulation; this REDUCES the scaling deposition rate and integral over the duty cycle.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
All components are existing or catalog classes; no new sensors; no fill inspection.

Row 1: Data Historian / SCADA Logic Module
(a) Catalog Class: Standard PLC/DCS logic routine or off-the-shelf data historian module.
(b) Function: Ingests existing water inlet/outlet temperature, flow, fan power, and existing conductivity logs. Computes rolling 7-day mean and standard deviation for approach ($\Delta T$) and conductivity ($\sigma$).
(c) Procurement Tag: (a) Existing control system upgrade; (b) Software license for standard trend-analytic module; (c) No new hardware.

Row 2: Thermal Flush Duty-Cycle Scheduler
(a) Catalog Class: Standard VSD (Variable Speed Drive) control logic module or relay logic in existing DCS.
(b) Function: When predictor triggers, commands existing fan VSDs and water pump VSDs to operate at 110% capacity for 4 hours, then 130% for 2 hours. This thermal shock and high shear scrub the fill.
(c) Procurement Tag: (a) Existing VSD firmware update; (b) No new hardware; (c) Electrical re-verification of existing overload protection.

Row 3: Existing Instrumentation Integration
(a) Catalog Class: No new devices.
(b) Function: Connects existing conductivity meter (stated in problem as existing log) and RTD sensors to the logic module.
(c) Procurement Tag: (a) Existing wiring; (b) No new sensors; (c) Signal isolation checks.

Row 4: Operational Cost Monitor
(a) Catalog Class: Standard energy monitoring dashboard module.
(b) Function: Logs the extra kWh consumed during the thermal flush and compares it to the cost of unscheduled fill cleaning or approach trip downtime.
(c) Procurement Tag: (a) Existing metering; (b) No new hardware; (c) Software configuration.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
Standard Practice Burden: Requires annual scaffolding, fill disassembly, chemical cleaning, and downtime. High operational loss during cleaning window.
This Mechanism Burden:
1. Installability: Zero new hardware. Software-only. SAME class, LOWER burden.
2. Operability: Automated. No manual intervention. SAME class, LOWER burden.
3. Maintenance: No new physical parts to maintain. SAME class, LOWER burden.
4. Operational Loss: The thermal flush adds ~50 kWh/tower per event (CALCULATED: 10% power increase for 4h + 30% for 2h at baseline 500 kW = 100 kWh). Frequency: ~4 events/year. Total extra energy: 400 kWh/year. Cost: ~$40/year (ASSUMPTION: $0.10/kWh). Downtime avoided: 1 shift (8h) of potential approach trip. Cost of trip: ~$5,000 in lost cooling efficiency and potential damage. Trade nets positive.
5. FA/Tower/Year: 0 FAs. All signals are existing. No new failure modes introduced.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol:
1. Retrieve 12 months of existing water quality and thermal data from the SCADA historian.
2. Identify 3 historical periods where the approach ($\Delta T$) drifted >2 C over 30 days, coinciding with conductivity drift >5%.
3. Apply the predictor logic to these historical periods.
4. Pass/Fail: The predictor must flag the period at least 30 days before the approach trip threshold (defined as $\Delta T$ > 37 C, ASSUMPTION based on 35 C design + 2 C margin).
5. Kill Criterion: If the predictor flags <30 days before trip in >1 of the 3 historical events, the mechanism is out of class.
6. Validation: Compare against existing maintenance logs that confirm fill cleaning was performed at those times.

CONSTRAINT BIND
Primary Stated Indicator: Water inlet/outlet temperature approach ($\Delta T$).
Secondary Stated Indicator: Conductivity (existing log).
The predictor uses $\Delta T$ as the primary failure driver indicator and conductivity as the supplement. Both are explicitly stated in the problem as existing. No new sensors. No fill inspection. No new hardware. The mechanism is a pure parameter/procedure change on existing equipment.
